title: CrewAI Pricing for 2026 and What Your Workload Costs
summary: CrewAI pricing includes free and hosted plans with execution limits from 50 to 30,000 monthly.
body_markdown:
## What CrewAI costs at realistic monthly usage


Three things make up your monthly bill: the plan fee, any flexible overage for runs beyond what the plan includes, and model-provider tokens billed separately. Runs are the metered unit, so the number to fix first is how many your workload fires each month.


To see this cost variable's maximum contribution before any free runs count, the table below takes three workloads and shows the most the $0.50 overage rate could add if the plan included no runs at all, which means you can see the overage cost ceiling.


Treat that as a ceiling. Every included run you find on the pricing page comes off the billable count, and the real overage is the gap between your runs and that allowance.


Scenario Runs per month Overage ceiling at $0.50 per run


Small team 500 $250


Production 2,000 $1,000


Move down the rows and the ceiling rises tenfold and then fourfold, because overage grows in a straight line with runs. Whatever allowance the plan carries only shifts that line down. It does not change its slope.


### Scenario 1: solo prototype on the free framework


At 50 runs a month, the open-source framework costs nothing to license. A solo builder running it on their own machine has no execution meter at all, which means developers at this volume have zero licensing costs.


On a hosted plan the worst case is $25 in overage, which is small enough that tokens will likely be the larger line, so token costs will be your primary spending concern.


Count how many model calls each run makes, multiply by your provider's per-token rate, and that's close to your whole bill.


One cost never shows up on an invoice: your own hours.


### Scenario 2: small team on a paid plan


At 500 runs, the plan question matters, meaning different tier choices now have significantly different financial implications.


Read the pricing page for how many runs the entry paid tier includes. If it covers all 500, overage is zero and you pay the fee. If it covers fewer, subtract the allowance from 500 and multiply the remainder by $0.50.


With a ceiling of $250, a plan whose allowance is close to your volume costs far less than that. Add your token estimate last and keep it as its own line, because it scales with model choice, not with the plan.


### CrewAI cost at production volume with overage


At 2,000 runs, overage is the line that can outgrow the fee. The $1,000 ceiling means a plan with a small allowance can cost many times its sticker price, while a higher tier with a large allowance may be cheaper overall.


Compare the two by working out the break-even: the extra fee for the higher tier divided by $0.50 gives the number of runs it must absorb to pay for itself, meaning you know when the upgrade becomes cost-justified.


Volume beyond that threshold makes the upgrade worthwhile.


Then add tokens, which at this volume are usually the largest charge of all.
